title: Snapshot
body:
On February 22, 2024, a six-legged lander named Odysseus touched down near the lunar south pole, became the first privately built spacecraft to land on the Moon, and announced the arrival of Intuitive Machines as something more than a NASA subcontractor with ambitions. The company had not gone public two years earlier with a particularly tidy story — a de-SPAC through Inflection Point Acquisition Corp in February 2023, a lumpy milestone-revenue accounting model, and the inherent operational risk of landing hardware on an airless body 238,000 miles away. But Odysseus changed the framing entirely.

## Company in Brief

Intuitive Machines (LUNR, NASDAQ) is headquartered in Houston, Texas, and was co-founded in 2013 by Stephen Altemus, who serves as Chief Executive Officer and President, and Dr. Kamal Ghaffarian, who serves as Chairman. Altemus came to the company directly from NASA Johnson Space Center, where he had served as Deputy Director and, in the aftermath of the February 2003 Columbia disaster, as Columbia Reconstruction Director — arguably the most operationally demanding aerospace-management role in the modern history of American human spaceflight. Ghaffarian, by the time Intuitive Machines was founded, had already built and sold Stinger Ghaffarian Technologies (subsequently acquired by KBR) and was simultaneously founding or chairing Axiom Space, X Energy, Quantum Space, and PTX. The founder-pair's NASA-institutional-credibility anchor and serial-entrepreneur capital-formation capability defined the company's early character.

The company's core product is the Nova-C class lunar lander, a vehicle designed to deliver scientific instruments, technology demonstrations, and commercial payloads to the lunar surface under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services program. NASA awarded Intuitive Machines a CLPS contract with a ceiling of $4.82 billion, with $150 million in near-term guaranteed value. The company is also developing the larger, cargo-class Nova-D lander; the $180.4 million IM-5 task order — the largest single CLPS award to date — calls for a Nova-D delivery to the Lunar South Pole.

## Financial Snapshot

Intuitive Machines' FY2025 financials reflected the inherent lumpiness of NASA milestone-payment revenue recognition. Fourth-quarter 2025 revenue came in at $44.8 million, down approximately 18 percent year-on-year, as IM-1 mission revenue had been substantially recognised in FY2024 and the company was in active preparation for subsequent missions. Full-year FY2025 revenue fell in the $250–$300 million range, with a Q4 gross margin of 19 percent — a workable figure for a capital-intensive aerospace developer, but not one that signalled operating-profitability inflection.

The inflection, management guided, was coming in FY2026. The company issued a revenue outlook of $900 million to $1 billion for the fiscal year ending December 2026, with positive Adjusted EBITDA — implying roughly 3–4x year-on-year revenue growth. Total backlog, post-Lanteris, stood at $943 million.

| Metric | FY2025 | FY2026 Outlook |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $250–300M | $900M–$1B |
| Q4 Gross Margin | 19% | — |
| Adj. EBITDA | Negative | Positive |
| Backlog | — | $943M (post-Lanteris) |

The dominant driver of that growth was a single transaction: the $800 million acquisition of Lanteris Space Systems, structured as $450 million cash and $350 million in stock, with an expected Q1 2026 close. Lanteris, led by Chris Johnson — previously President of Boeing Satellite Systems International — brought Boeing-pedigree satellite systems capability into the Intuitive Machines portfolio. Johnson assumed the title of President of Lanteris Space Systems within the combined company. The acquisition's strategic logic was explicit: Intuitive Machines was transforming from a lunar logistics specialist into a full space prime contractor with the satellite systems capability to compete for the broadest category of civil and national-security space programmes.

## Board and Governance

The six-director board that oversaw this transformation was unusually credentialled for a small-cap space company. Ghaffarian and Altemus anchored it as co-founders. William Liquori, a retired Lieutenant General and former Chief Strategy and Resourcing Officer of the U.S. Space Force, supplied the Pentagon procurement signal. Robert Masson — U.S. Naval Academy, Harvard MBA, ex-Raytheon CFO, Naval Aviator — chaired the Audit Committee. Michael Blitzer, founder of Kingstown Capital and the original Inflection Point SPAC sponsor who brought LUNR public, chaired Strategic Transactions, the committee that approved the Lanteris deal. Nicole Seligman — Harvard College and Harvard Law School both magna cum laude, former President of Sony Entertainment and Sony Corporation of America, former Global General Counsel of Sony Corporation, former clerk to Justice Thurgood Marshall, and a sitting OpenAI board director — provided corporate-governance credentialling of a depth rarely seen at a company of LUNR's market capitalisation.

## Central Tension

The company that presented itself to investors in the spring of 2026 had demonstrated lunar-landing capability twice — IM-1's Odysseus in February 2024 and IM-2's Athena in Q1 2025, both of which reached the lunar surface with operational complications but completed their primary mission objectives. It was executing the largest acquisition in its history. It was guiding to near-decadal revenue growth in a single fiscal year. Three questions remained open: whether the NASA Artemis programme would sustain the lunar economy thesis through the late 2020s at a pace sufficient to justify the CLPS contract ceiling; whether the Lanteris integration would deliver the space-prime-contractor positioning its price tag demanded; and whether IM-3, IM-4, and IM-5 would execute cleanly enough to validate the operational-execution model the entire investment case depended upon.
